stacked.headline: The €30 "gift" rose at your Promenade café table.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Nice rose scam: "a rose for the beautiful lady" costs €30
stacked.pin_description: On Promenade des Anglais terraces and outdoor cafés in Vieux Nice, a vendor places a "free" rose in the woman's hand or on the table — then loudly demands €10–€30, banking on public embarrassment. Don't touch it, don't let it land. Say "Non merci" loudly; ask staff to remove the vendor ("on n'a rien commandé"). Tabiji's France scam guide.

stacked.headline: The Vieux Nice ATM that drained €800 in Lyon.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Nice ATM skim: card jammed in Vieux Nice, €800 drained in Lyon
stacked.pin_description: On dim Vieux Nice side streets, ATMs get card-reader overlays that read your stripe and fake keypads that record your PIN. Variant: a false-slot insert jams your card; a scammer retrieves it later with your PIN. €800 charge appears in Lyon overnight. Use bank-lobby ATMs only — BNP Paribas, Société Générale, Crédit Agricole or CIC, during business hours. Cover the keypad. From Tabiji's France scam guide.

hook.pin_description: Vieux Nice side-street ATMs run skimmer overlays and card-trap inserts. The screen reads "Carte Bloquée," a "helpful" stranger urges you to retry the PIN, and €800 hits your card overnight from Lyon. Use only ATMs inside BNP Paribas, Société Générale, Crédit Agricole or CIC during business hours. Tabiji's France scam guide.

stacked.headline: "For you, Madame! A gift!" — then €20 demanded.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Marseille friendship bracelet scam — the slip-knot trap at the Old Port
stacked.pin_description: At the Vieux-Port, a smiling stranger grabs your wrist and knots a colored string before you can pull back. The slip-knot tightens when tugged, and €5 to €20 is demanded for the "gift" while an accomplice lifts your wallet from behind. Keep both hands in your front pockets, say "Non, merci" without breaking stride, and step into the nearest shop if grabbed.

Panel 4: she walks past, ignoring him as he tries again on another tourist couple. Caption reads "A firm 'Non!' is the best defense."

hook.hook: "For you, Madame! A gift!"
hook.pin_title: How the Marseille bracelet scam opens — "For you, Madame! A gift!"
hook.pin_description: It always starts as a gift. At the Vieux-Port and along La Canebière, scammers knot a slip-knot string onto your wrist before you can react, then demand €20 while a partner picks your pocket. Keep your hands in your front pockets and answer "Non, merci" without slowing down. Real Marseillais don't tie strings on strangers.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel showing a young man in a striped shirt approaching an older woman in a straw hat at Marseille's Vieux-Port harbor, holding out a tangle of colored strings and saying "For you, Madame! A gift!" Sailboats and pastel harbor buildings fill the background.

lesson.lesson: A firm "Non!" is the best defense.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Marseille bracelet scam — a firm "Non!" is the best defense
lesson.pin_description: If a stranger reaches for your wrist near the Vieux-Port, you don't owe them politeness. Cross your arms over your chest, say "Non, merci" once, and keep walking. Step into a shop or hotel lobby if they follow. The slip-knot tightens once it's on, and €20 turns into €5 to €20 plus whatever an accomplice lifts from your back pocket.

stacked.pin_description: A scammer near the Vieux-Port "finds" a fake-stamped brass ring on the ground and offers it as a lucky gift, then asks for €10 to €30 as a finder's reward. While you examine the ring, an accomplice lifts your wallet or phone from behind. Don't stop, don't take it. Say "Non, ce n'est pas a moi" and keep moving.

hook.hook: "You dropped this! It must be your lucky day."
hook.pin_title: Marseille gold ring scam — "You dropped this! It must be your lucky day."
hook.pin_description: If anyone near the Vieux-Port "finds" a gold ring at your feet, it's brass and it isn't yours. The fee comes after the smile: €10 to €30 in cash plus whatever a partner lifts from your back pocket. Keep walking. Real lost rings get handed to a shop or to the police municipale, not to passing strangers.

Carry your wallet in a front pocket or money belt while in tourist zones from La Canebière to Gare Saint-Charles, where the same crew rotates between drops.

stacked.pin_description: On Métro Line 1 and around Gare Saint-Charles, child crews push a cardboard sign at chest height to block your sightline while an accomplice lifts your wallet or phone. The metro door-close moment is peak theft. Wear a cross-body bag in front, never sling it on a chair, and keep phones out of back pockets, especially at the Vieux-Port and La Canebière.

hook.pin_description: On Métro Line 1 and around the Vieux-Port, a sudden child-crowd with a clipboard is the distraction; the lift happens behind your back. Keep your bag zipped and in front, especially as the metro doors close. Phones belong in front pockets, not back.

Cross-body bag worn in front, hand resting on the zipper, no phones in back pockets, and step away the moment a small crowd materializes around you. lesson.pin_description: Use ATMs inside a bank lobby during business hours. Wiggle the card slot — skimmers are glued, real readers are bolted. Cover the keypad with your other hand. If your card jams, do not leave; call the bank emergency number printed on the ATM, then file a Plainte with Police Nationale within 24 hours.

stacked.headline: "We must check for counterfeit money." They are not police.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Marseille fake police scam — "counterfeit" wallet checks that pocket €100 to €500
stacked.pin_description: Two-man "plainclothes Tourist Police" teams flash a fake badge for half a second and demand to inspect your wallet for "counterfeit euros." While you watch one hand, the other palms €100 to €500 in cash. Real French police carry a carte professionnelle and never inspect wallets on the street. Insist on continuing at the nearest commissariat. Call 17 or 112 if pushed.

hook.pin_title: Marseille fake-police scam — "Tourist Police. Counterfeit money check."
hook.pin_description: France has no "Tourist Police." The badge flash lasts under a second on purpose. Ask for the carte professionnelle and say "On va au commissariat" — real officers comply, scammers walk off.

lesson.pin_description: Real French fines are issued in writing on a procès-verbal with a payment slip — never in cash on the spot. If anyone in plainclothes wants to inspect your wallet, refuse and call 17 (Police) or 112 (urgences). File a Plainte at any commissariat the same day for a paper trail.

stacked.pin_description: A stranger near the Vieux-Port points out fake bird droppings (toothpaste, sauce, or hair gel) on your jacket, then offers to clean it while a partner lifts your wallet from your bag. Don't let strangers touch your clothes. Step back, walk 50 metres, and clean the stain in a café or hotel lobby once you've checked your bag.

stacked.pin_description: Crews stake out Calanques trailhead and Prado beach parking, identifying rental cars by plate, sterile interior, and visible bags. Windows are smashed within 10 to 60 minutes — one documented case stripped a car in 10. A broken quarter-window costs €300 to €800 against your damage deposit. Drop suitcases at the hotel before sightseeing, leave the trunk visibly empty, and use attended parking.

hook.pin_description: At Calanques trailheads and Prado beach lots, crews read your plate before you've finished locking the door. Anything visible — empty backpack, charger cable, sunglasses case — gets a window broken. Empty trunk only. Always.

lesson.pin_title: Marseille rentals — never leave bags visible
lesson.pin_description: At Calanques parking and Prado beaches: trunk visibly empty, doors locked at every red light on the corniche, passport on your person. Use attended lots (€5 to €15 premium) when possible. If hit, photograph damage and file a Plainte with Police Nationale within 24 hours for the rental insurance claim.

stacked.headline: "Wire €630 — we save the Airbnb fee." The flat doesn't exist.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Marseille Airbnb scam — phantom listings and €630 wire transfers
stacked.pin_description: Phantom Marseille listings advertised at €90/night (vs. €180+ market) push you to wire €630 directly to an IBAN "to save fees." Photos are stolen from real listings in other cities. On arrival, the address is wrong or the building has no such unit. Book only on Airbnb / Booking.com / VRBO checkout, pay by credit card, and reverse-image-search photos before paying.

hook.pin_description: If the host pushes you off-platform to a wire transfer, the apartment doesn't exist. Reverse-image-search the listing photos. If they appear in Lyon, Lisbon, or Athens, walk away.

lesson.pin_description: Stay inside the Airbnb / Booking.com / VRBO checkout flow and pay by credit card for chargeback rights. Verify the address on Google Street View. Refuse "let's handle off-platform" messages and IBAN wires. If you've already paid, file a Plainte with Police Nationale and dispute the card or bank wire same day.

stacked.headline: "Quick swim!" Bag gone in 60 seconds.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Marseille Prado beach theft — the 60-second towel-pile lift
stacked.pin_description: On Prado beaches and the Calanques, thieves wait for tourists to walk to the water and lift the entire towel pile — phone, wallet, hotel key — in a 60-second window. Pair-team variants engage you in English about the view while a partner walks off with your belongings. Bring only what you can lose, use a waterproof neck pouch in the water, or pay €15 to €25 for a beach-club lounger with staff watch.

hook.pin_title: Marseille Prado beach theft — "Tourist bag — easy!"
hook.pin_description: On Prado, your towel is a billboard: phone outline, hotel key, leather wallet. The lift takes 60 seconds while you're swimming. Take turns watching the bag, or never bring it at all.

lesson.pin_description: On Prado and the Calanques, leave passports, watches, and laptops in the hotel safe. Bring a waterproof neck pouch with phone, one card, and €20 cash, and swim with it. Beach-locker rentals run €3 to €5/day. Pay €15 to €25 for a private beach-club lounger if you're alone.

Wear cross-body bags in front, keep phones out of back pockets, and stay especially alert during Métro Line D and T2 door-open windows. Call 17 if surrounded.

hook.pin_description: When a stranger asks for directions on Place Bellecour, somebody's hand is already on your bag. Keep walking, point in a direction, never stop and unfold a map in a crowd. Métro Line D door-close is the highest-risk moment.

stacked.headline: "I'll help with the machine!" The ticket is already used.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Lyon fake metro ticket scam — "helpful" strangers at Part-Dieu and Perrache
stacked.pin_description: At Part-Dieu and Perrache, touts offer "discounted" TCL tickets at €1 to €1.50 (real fare €2). The ticket is expired or already used; the gate rejects it after the seller disappears, and inspectors fine you €40+ for fraud. Always buy from official TCL machines, counters, or the TCL app — and use contactless tap-to-pay (€2 single, €6.30 day pass, €17.10 carnet of 10).

lesson.pin_description: Buy at staffed TCL counters, the TCL app, or contactless tap-to-pay at the turnstile. Real prices: €2 single, €6.30 day pass, €17.10 carnet of 10. Set the machine language to English with the top-right button. If you bought a fake, file a Plainte within 24 hours.

After signing, they flip to a "donation" page and demand €5 to €20 cash while a partner picks pockets. Real French charities collect emails at staffed stalls. Say "non, merci" without breaking stride.

stacked.pin_description: On Rue Mercière and in Vieux Lyon, uncertified "bouchons" hand English menus priced €5 to €15 above French ones, add €4 to €6 "couvert" charges for unordered bread or amuse-bouche, and push €7 Évian instead of free tap water. Card terminals pre-fill 18% tips. Eat at certified Authentique Bouchon Lyonnais venues, ask for "une carafe d'eau," and check the bill.

lesson.pin_description: By French law, tap water ("carafe d'eau") is free and service is included. Compare the French and English menus before ordering, ask the price of any "daily special," and decline the pre-filled tip. Eat at certified Authentique Bouchon Lyonnais — the label is at the door.

stacked.pin_description: At Lyon café terraces near Place des Terreaux and the Saône / Rhône quays, sunset rose vendors place a "free" rose on your table, then demand €5 to €30 once you've touched it. lesson.pin_description: Hands at your sides or in your lap. Loud "non, merci" without smiling. If the rose is already on the table, ask the waiter to remove it — "on n'a rien commandé." Same play runs at Place des Terreaux and the Saône quays with bracelets and "lucky charm" pendants.

stacked.headline: "Pardon, can you change a 50 euro note?" Then "police" arrive.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Lyon fake-police scam — the currency exchange trap at Bellecour metro
stacked.pin_description: Near Bellecour metro and Lyon nightlife, an "accomplice tourist" asks you to break a €50 note. Two fake plainclothes "police" then arrive claiming "street currency exchange is illegal" and demanding wallet inspection. €100 to €500 vanishes from your wallet during the inspection. Real French police never inspect wallets on the street — only documents.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic at Lyon's Bellecour metro entrance. Panel 1: a young man approaches an older male tourist with shoulder bag, holding up a green €50 note and saying "Pardon, can you change a 50 euro note?" Panel 3: the tourist looks into a near-empty wallet and exclaims "Hey! My money...

hook.hook: "Pardon, can you change a 50 euro note?"
hook.pin_title: Lyon fake-police hook — "Pardon, can you change a 50 euro note?"
hook.pin_description: The change request near Bellecour metro is the cue for the fake "police" to arrive 30 seconds later. France has no Tourist Police, no street wallet inspections, no on-the-spot cash fines. "Non, désolé" and walk on.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel of a young man holding up a green €50 note to an older male tourist with shoulder bag near the Bellecour metro entrance in Lyon, asking "Pardon, can you change a 50 euro note?"

lesson.lesson: Real police never inspect cash on the street.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Lyon fake police — real police never inspect cash on the street
lesson.pin_description: Real officers carry a carte professionnelle with photo and badge number, and they hand it over for inspection. Insist on continuing at the nearest commissariat: "nous allons au commissariat ensemble." If pushed, call 17 (Police) or 112 (urgences). File a Plainte the same day.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel of a uniformed Police Nationale officer pointing at an older man with shoulder bag outside a Lyon Police station, with the caption "Real police never inspect cash on the street."

stacked.headline: "€110? My app says €60." The meter wasn't on.

stacked.pin_description: From Lyon-Saint Exupéry (LYS), Part-Dieu, and Perrache, drivers "forget" to start the meter or switch to night-rate "Tarif B" during weekday daytime. €100 quoted vs. €50 to €70 official. Confirm "Tarif A" on display, demand the meter ("au compteur, s'il vous plaît"), or use the Rhônexpress tram (€17.10 single, €30.50 round-trip) from LYS to Part-Dieu in 30 minutes.

Panel 2: in the back of the cab she leans forward and tells the driver "Excuse me, the meter isn't on." Panel 4: a.

hook.hook: "Excuse me, the meter isn't on."
hook.pin_title: Lyon taxi scam — "Excuse me, the meter isn't on."
hook.pin_description: The moment you leave the airport curb without a running meter, the price is whatever the driver says at arrival. Display should show "A" daytime, never "B" before evening. €50 to €70 is the real range.

lesson.pin_title: Lyon taxis — always confirm the meter is running
lesson.pin_description: Use only marked taxi ranks at LYS, Part-Dieu, and Perrache. Confirm "Tarif A," demand a receipt and a credit card terminal (both legally required), and use Uber / Bolt for upfront pricing. Photograph the carte professionnelle if overcharged; the prefecture handles complaints.

stacked.headline: "Accept conversion? 1 EUR = 0.90 USD" — that's the trap.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Lyon ATM scam — yellow Euronet ATMs near Part-Dieu and the DCC "convenient rate"
stacked.pin_description: Near Lyon's Part-Dieu and tourist streets, yellow Euronet / Travelex ATMs offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at a 5 to 8% worse rate plus €4 to €8 fees. A €100 withdrawal becomes $124 vs. $108 at a bank ATM. Always select "Decline conversion" or "Charge in EUR" and use ATMs inside BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL, or Crédit Agricole lobbies.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic in Lyon. Panel 1: a young female tourist with a backpack approaches a yellow standalone "ATM" outside Part-Dieu station, saying "Just need a few euros for a taxi." Panel 2: the ATM screen shows a large prompt "Accept conversion to USD? Rate: 1 EUR = 0.90 USD — ACCEPT / DECLINE" and the speech bubble reads "Accept our convenient rate?" Panel 3: she frowns at her banking app reading the actual fees on her phone and says "That's not convenient,

hook.hook: "Accept our convenient rate?"
hook.pin_title: Lyon ATM scam — "Accept our convenient rate?"
hook.pin_description: On a Lyon Euronet ATM, the DCC "convenient rate" is 5 to 8% worse than your card issuer's. €100 turns into $124 instead of $108. Always tap "Decline conversion / Charge in EUR."
hook.alt_text: Comic panel of a yellow ATM screen showing "Accept conversion to USD? Rate: 1 EUR = 0.90 USD" with ACCEPT / DECLINE buttons, and a voice asking "Accept our convenient rate?"

lesson.lesson: Always decline conversion and use bank ATMs.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Lyon ATMs — always decline conversion and use bank ATMs
lesson.pin_description: Use only ATMs inside French bank lobbies during business hours: BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL, Crédit Agricole. Wiggle the card slot before inserting (skimmers are glued, real readers bolted). Cover the keypad. If the card jams, don't leave; call the bank emergency number from the ATM itself.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel of a young woman in a sunhat walking past a green Crédit Agricole bank branch ATM in Lyon, with Notre-Dame de Fourvière visible on the hill behind. Caption reads "Always decline conversion and use bank ATMs."

stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Lyon broken camera scam — the €300 "repair fee" at Fourvière
stacked.pin_description: At the Fourvière viewpoint, a friendly "tourist" asks you to take their photo with an old DSLR. When you hand it back, they shout "You broke it!" and demand €100 to €500 in cash for repairs. The camera was already broken — same prop, same script, all day. Decline politely; offer to use your phone instead. Suggest filing a police report together — they'll vanish.

Panel 3: he points an angry finger at her demanding "You must pay! Three hundred euros!" while a small crowd watches.

hook.hook: "Excusez-moi, a photo please?"
hook.pin_title: Lyon broken camera scam — "Excusez-moi, a photo please?"
hook.pin_description: Real owners of expensive cameras don't hand them to strangers. At Fourvière, the camera is already broken before you hold it — €100 to €500 in "repairs" is the play. Point at your phone: "use yours, mine has the same camera."

lesson.lesson: The safest photo is the one you don't take.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Lyon broken camera scam — the safest photo is the one you don't take
lesson.pin_description: If you're accused of breaking a stranger's camera, suggest going to the police together: "nous allons porter plainte ensemble." Real victims agree; scammers walk off. Pay nothing on the spot. If they block your path, call Police Nationale 17.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel of an older female tourist in a straw hat and red scarf walking calmly along a Fourvière viewpoint parapet in Lyon with the city's red rooftops spread behind her. Caption reads "The safest photo is the one you don't take."

Two minutes later a moped passes twice — the rear rider grabs your wrist, twists the clasp, and a third crew member drops tear gas to stop pursuit. Leave watches over $5K at home or in the hotel safe. Wear a Casio in public; gendarmerie 17 if attacked.

hook.pin_title: He photographed your wrist. The moped is two minutes behind. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: On La Croisette during festival weeks, spotter crews photograph wrists at hotel terraces and signal moped snatchers waiting two streets away. The 2024 Cannes Film Festival saw multiple seven-figure watch thefts at the Carlton, Martinez and Majestic. If a stranger photographs you or compliments the watch, change your route immediately.

lesson.pin_description: Cleanest defense against the Cannes moped-snatch crews is to never wear the real watch outdoors. Keep luxury pieces for indoor private events you arrived at by car, sit with your back to the wall on terraces, and confirm travel insurance covers jewelry up to full value before the trip.

stacked.pin_description: Prefecture-set fares: €85 weekday, €105 night/Sunday/holiday, plus €1.50 per extra bag. Scam drivers start the meter at €85 and let it keep ticking. Confirm the rate verbally before bags go in the trunk, photograph the meter at start and end, and insist on a card receipt. Train from Nice-Ville to Cannes is €7.30 every 20 minutes.

hook.pin_description: The €85 was indeed the prefecture-set fixed rate from Nice Airport to Cannes — but the meter should have been switched to that mode and locked, not started at €85 and allowed to keep accumulating. Then the driver claims the card machine is broken to force cash with no receipt.

lesson.pin_title: Photograph the meter. Card receipt only. €85 fixed. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: If the driver claims the card machine is broken, get out and take the next taxi. Uber and Bolt run Nice→Cannes with upfront fares. stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes pickpocket teams: 3 people, 1 map, 15 seconds | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: A 'lost tourist' asks for the Hôtel Splendid with a paper map at chest height. Two crew members step into your blind spots — backpack zips open, phone slides out, wallet leaves a back pocket. Wear backpacks on your front in any Cannes crowd; treat any close-distance direction request as an active distraction.

But she just needed…' Panel 4: Sitting at a café terrace with palm trees, the woman holds her bag firmly across her lap and says 'A.

hook.pin_description: The chest-height clipboard or map is the diagnostic. At chest height your eyes look down and your peripheral vision can't track your own pockets. Real Niçois ask for directions from a comfortable two-meter distance — anyone closer is reading your pockets.

lesson.pin_title: Cannes rule: backpack on the front. Hand on the bag. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: If something is spilled on you, walk fifty meters away from the helpful stranger before addressing the stain — the spill is the cue, not a coincidence. Step into a hotel lobby if surrounded; the crew won't follow into a venue with cameras. Gendarmerie 17 if blocked.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: A woman in a yellow sunhat and red scarf sits at a Cannes café terrace with palm trees and the sea behind her. She holds her crossbody handbag firmly closed across her lap with one hand and says 'A helping hand needs a zipped-up bag.'

stacked.pin_description: Multi-language clipboards near the Palais raise to chest height to break your sightline while an accomplice lifts your wallet from behind. stacked.pin_title: Cannes seabass at €12? It was per 100g. Real bill: €72. | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Tourist-trap menus in Le Suquet and around the Palais hide 'prix au 100g' fish footnotes, push verbal 'specials' with no price, and run dual menus where English costs €5–€15 more than French. Always ask 'le prix du plat du jour, s'il vous plaît' and verify whether fish is per 100g or per portion.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: A waiter in vest and bowtie hands a menu to a woman in a sunhat at a Cannes terrasse: 'Our house specials, madame!' Panel 2: Close-up of an open menu — every dish reads 'market price' beside it; the woman looks alarmed: 'No prices on the menu!' Panel 3: She holds the bill: 'Ninety euros for lunch?!' as the waiter stands silent. Panel 4: The same woman now stands beside a clear chalkboard with all dishes priced at 12€ and points: 'Always check posted prices first!'

hook.hook: Every line of the menu says 'market price.' That's the whole trick.
hook.pin_title: Every line says 'market price.' That's the whole trick. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: When a Cannes terrasse menu hides prices behind 'market price' or 'prix au 100g' you're being set up for bill shock. Order 'carafe d'eau' for free water, watch for 'couvert' or 'service' lines, and decline pre-filled tip percentages on the card terminal.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: A woman in a yellow sunhat and red scarf sits at a Cannes terrasse table with a glass of wine while a waiter in a black vest and bowtie hands her a leather menu. Speech bubble from the waiter: 'Our house specials, madame!' Stone Cannes townhouses line the street behind them.

lesson.lesson: Ask for the French menu. Confirm 'prix au 100g' before saying yes. Read reviews before sitting down.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: French menu first. Per-100g vs per-portion. Reviews before sitting. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: Reputable Cannes spots — La Palme d'Or, La Mère Besson, Astoux et Brun for shellfish — are transparent. Eat one block off La Croisette or away from the Palais and prices drop 30–40%. Worst offenders have consistent one-star reviews citing the exact tactics.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: A woman in a yellow sunhat stands beside a wooden chalkboard menu where every line reads '12€' clearly. She gestures to the board with one hand — caption: 'Always check posted prices first!' A red-checked Italian-style awning is visible behind her.

stacked.headline: Real French police never ask to see your wallet on the street. Ever.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes fake-cop wallet check: real police never do this | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Plainclothes 'officers' near Cannes ATMs flash a badge and demand your wallet to inspect for 'counterfeit euros.' They thumb through cash and palm €100–€300. Show only a passport photocopy, demand to see the 'carte professionnelle,' and insist on continuing at the commissariat. 17 (police) or 112 (EU emergency) if escalated.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: Two men in plainclothes flank a grey-bearded tourist on a Cannes promenade — 'Excuse me, sir. Police.' Panel 2: One of them holds up a 'POLICE NATIONALE' ID card while reaching for the tourist's open wallet — 'We must check for counterfeit euros.' Panel 3: The two men walk away into the crowd as the tourist checks his empty wallet — 'Hey! My money is gone!' Panel 4: A real uniformed gendarme in képi shows the tourist a proper carte professionnelle in front of a Police.

hook.hook: He flashed the badge for half a second. Then asked for your wallet to 'check counterfeits.'
hook.pin_title: He flashed the badge for half a second. Then asked for your wallet. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: Real French police only verify identity documents (passport, ID card), and any wallet inspection is conducted at a station, not curbside. Crews work near ATMs along Rue d'Antibes, the Palais during festival weeks, and the Vieux Port boardwalk. Some variants use a 'tourist accomplice' to add plausibility.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: On a Cannes seafront promenade with palm trees and the bay behind, two men in dark suits flank a grey-bearded tourist with a leather satchel. The taller one in front holds up a hand and says 'Excuse me, sir. Police.'

lesson.lesson: Show a passport copy. Ask for the carte professionnelle. Insist on going to the commissariat together.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Passport copy only. 'Nous allons au commissariat ensemble.' | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: Real officers will agree without resistance; scammers will lose interest and walk off. If the encounter started with a 'tourist' asking to break a bill, refuse — the 'officers' never appear if the accomplice's setup doesn't land. Call 17 or 112 if they block your path.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: A real uniformed gendarme in dark blue uniform and képi shows a proper carte professionnelle ID badge to a grey-bearded tourist in front of a marked Police Nationale car. Caption: 'Real police never check cash on the street.'

stacked.headline: He asked for the museum. He was reading your PIN over your shoulder.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes ATM shimming: paper-thin chip cloners + pinhole cameras | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Standalone ATMs near Gare de Cannes get fitted with paper-thin shims inside the card slot and pinhole cameras above the keypad. The crew streams chip + PIN to a phone in a café. Use bank-lobby ATMs (BNP Paribas, Société Générale, Crédit Agricole, CIC), wiggle the slot before inserting, and cover the keypad.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: At a Cannes street ATM a tourist in a striped shirt with a paper map asks a grey-bearded man at the machine 'Excuse me — where is the museum?' Panel 2: A second man has joined behind, leaning in toward the keypad — 'Just show me the street name!' the tourist with the map insists. Panel 3: At his hotel the grey-bearded man stares at his phone showing 'BANK ALERT: €500 WITHDRAWN' — caption: 'Five hundred euros withdrawn!' Panel 4: Inside a 'CANNES BANK' lobby a smiling.

hook.hook: He asked for the museum at the exact moment you typed your PIN. That wasn't coincidence.
hook.pin_title: He asked for the museum the second you typed your PIN. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: Shimming is the 2020s upgrade to skimming — a paper-thin shim inside the slot reads chip data as your card slides past, and a pinhole camera captures your PIN. Some shims have Bluetooth so the crew never has to retrieve the device. The data streams to a phone fifty meters away.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: At a Cannes street ATM with palm trees behind, a tourist in a striped shirt holds up a paper map and asks a grey-bearded man at the keypad 'Excuse me — where is the museum?' The grey-bearded man, in a leather satchel and cap, has paused mid-transaction.

lesson.lesson: Bank-lobby ATMs only. Wiggle the slot. Cover the keypad. Enable transaction-alert SMS.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Bank-lobby ATMs only. Wiggle the slot. SMS alerts on. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: Skimmer overlays detach with a firm tug because they're glued not bolted. If your card jams, do NOT leave the machine — call your bank from the ATM. After a confirmed skim, freeze the card via the bank app and file a Plainte with Police Nationale within 24 hours.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: Inside a brightly lit 'CANNES BANK' lobby with potted plants, a smiling teller in a navy blazer gestures toward an indoor ATM where a grey-bearded man cups one hand over the keypad as he types. Speech bubble from the teller: 'Always cover the keypad!'

stacked.headline: 'Let's pay outside Airbnb to save the fee.' That's the entire scam.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes Festival rental fraud: 'pay outside Airbnb' = no apartment | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Phantom listings during Film Festival, Cannes Lions and Yachting Festival weeks at €280/night when comparable units run €600+ ask you to wire to a private IBAN to 'save fees.' Photos are stolen from real Lyon Airbnbs. Off-platform payment voids protection. Reverse-image-search photos with Google Lens before booking.

A FESTIVAL CANNES poster hangs above her desk. Panel 2: With a backpack and wheelie suitcase she stands outside a stone Cannes building checking her phone — 'This must be the place…' Panel 3: A uniformed concierge with a clipboard at the building's lobby tells her: 'Madame, this apartment is not for rent.' Panel 4: She sits dejected on a bare bed in an empty.

hook.hook: €280/night during Film Festival when everyone else is €600+. The 'host' wants a wire transfer.
hook.pin_title: €280/night when everyone else is €600+. Wire transfer requested. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: Film Festival week (mid-May), Cannes Lions (mid-June) and Yachting Festival (early September) are peak fraud windows because demand spikes prices 4–8× and the resulting 'deals' pull the most victims. New host with thin reviews, urgency, prices 30–50% below market, off-platform request — all diagnostic.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: A woman in an orange t-shirt sits at a wooden desk typing on a laptop. A bright 'FESTIVAL CANNES' poster with palm trees hangs on the wall behind her. A chat bubble from a 'host' avatar on the laptop reads 'Pay by bank transfer to secure it.'

lesson.lesson: Only Airbnb / VRBO / Booking.com checkout. Never wire. Never PayPal friends-and-family. Reverse-image-search photos.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Inside the app only. Reverse-image-search every photo. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: For Film Festival or Yachting Festival weeks, book 6–9 months ahead through established hotels (Carlton, Martinez, Majestic, Splendid). Pay by credit card so chargeback layers on top of platform protection. Treat any 'let's handle this directly' message as immediate cancel-and-report.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: A woman in an orange t-shirt sits dejected on the edge of a bare bed in an empty Cannes room with peeling wallpaper, holding her phone in one hand. Her backpack rests on the dusty floor. Caption: 'Lesson learned. Always pay inside the app.'

stacked.headline: Festival accreditation is free for industry. It is never resold on Instagram.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes Festival pass scam: real badges aren't sold on Instagram | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Fake 'Cannes Festival Tickets' accounts sell €1,500 'Marché du Film badges' and €600 Carlton after-party invites. None are real. Accreditation is free, non-transferable, and only via festival-cannes.com. After-parties go through agencies and personal networks, never DMs.

Panel 2: The buyer hands over euros while clutching the fake pass: 'Enjoy the red carpet!' Panel 3: At the festival barricade with red banners, a uniformed gendarme inspects the pass and tells him 'This credential is fake!' Panel 4: At an official 'BILLETERIE OFFICIELLE' window,

hook.pin_description: A real Marché du Film badge is tied to a verified industry email and photo ID, and cannot be sold. The 'festival internship' angle targets film students with €2,000–€5,000 packages promising 'festival experience' that turns out to be a self-arranged trip with no industry access.

lesson.lesson: festival-cannes.com is the only official URL. Real internships pay students — not the other way around.

lesson.pin_description: Verify any film festival via the IMDb festival database, FilmFreeway's verified-festival list, or the Festival Alliance directory. Pay with a credit card so chargebacks are possible. Cannes-area gendarmerie handles festival-fraud reports — call 17.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: At an official 'BILLETERIE OFFICIELLE' Cannes ticket window with the festival's golden palm-leaf logo on banners, a uniformed staff member in blue hands a real credential to a customer with a camera. Speech bubble: 'Only official credentials!'

stacked.headline: €15K wired to a Latvian IBAN. The Sunseeker doesn't exist.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes yacht charter fraud: €15K deposit, no boat, no office | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: 'Charter' websites advertise a 30-meter Sunseeker at 30–50% below market with mobile-only contact and no MYBA or ECPY membership. Photos are lifted from real Croatian charters; IBANs are in Latvia. Book only through MYBA or ECPY brokers, use BoatBookings or Camper & Nicholsons escrow, visit the boat at port before final payment.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: A man at a desk in a cap is on the phone in front of a laptop showing a yacht photo: '€15,000 deposit? Sounds like a deal!' Panel 2: Same man at the laptop confirms a wire transfer; an inset shows the scammer's email reading 'Must transfer today to hold the dates!' next to a green CONFIRM button — caption: 'Okay, the wire transfer is sent.' Panel 3: At Port de Cannes with sailboats, the man stares at his phone: 'No boat? No office? The number is dead.' Panel 4: Inside.

hook.hook: 30-meter Sunseeker, €25K/week, €15K wire 'this week' — only mobile, only Gmail.
hook.pin_title: Sunseeker, €15K wire, only mobile, only Gmail. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: Five-figure deposits and same-week timeline pressure feel normal in the yacht industry — that's why it's a high-margin fraud target. Scam tells: only mobile contact, no MYBA or ECPY membership, prices 30–50% below market, refusal to use escrow, pressure to wire to overseas IBANs.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: A grey-bearded man in a cap and casual shirt sits at a wooden desk, phone to ear, looking at a laptop screen showing a luxury yacht photo. He smiles broadly and says '€15,000 deposit? Sounds like a deal!' Bookshelves and a small framed picture are visible behind him.

lesson.lesson: Verify on myba.net / ecpy.org. Use BoatBookings or Camper & Nicholsons escrow. Visit the boat before final payment.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: myba.net + ecpy.org check. Escrow only. Visit the boat. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: Verify the vessel's IMO number on Equasis or the French Direction des Affaires Maritimes registry. Pay any final balance by credit card. After fraud, file a Plainte with Police Nationale and report to the gendarmerie maritime within 48 hours — required for insurance recourse.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: Inside the Capitainerie at Port de Cannes, a port officer in a navy uniform points to two posters on the wall — one shows the blue 'MYBA' logo with a sailboat, the other a yellow 'ECPY' badge. Caption: 'Always use a real, accredited yacht broker.' A grey-bearded customer with a backpack listens.

stacked.headline: 90 minutes at the beach. Quarter-window smashed. Trunk empty.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cannes rental break-ins: trunk empty inside 60 minutes | tabiji.ai
stacked.pin_description: Crews stake out Plage du Midi, Plage Macé, Pointe Croisette, Esterel trailheads (Pic du Cap Roux, Théoule) and Corniche d'Or pull-offs. They ID rentals by sticker, plate and GPS suction marks, and time break-ins to the middle of your visit. Check into the hotel before any sightseeing — drive trunk-empty.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: A woman in a sunhat opens the rear of a small white rental car parked under palms — backpack visible inside — saying 'Quick coffee stop!' Panel 2: Two hooded figures peer through the same car's window — caption: 'Tourist rental — easy grab.' Panel 3: The woman returns holding a coffee cup and stares at the car's smashed rear window with glass on the road — 'They broke the window!' Panel 4: At a 'POLICE MUNICIPALE de Cannes' desk a uniformed officer types on a computer.

hook.hook: Rental sticker, foreign plate, GPS suction marks. They watched you load the trunk.
hook.pin_title: Rental sticker, foreign plate, GPS suction marks. They were watching. | Cannes
hook.pin_description: France has one of the highest car break-in rates in Western Europe; the Cannes-Nice-Monaco corridor and Esterel access points are the busiest single zones. Crews know average tourist visit times — beach 2–4 hours, hiking trail 60–120 minutes — and time the smash for the middle of the window.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: A woman in a sunhat, sunglasses and an orange shirt stands at the open rear door of a small white rental car parked on a Cannes street with palm trees. Inside the car a black backpack is clearly visible on the seat. Speech bubble: 'Quick coffee stop!'

lesson.lesson: Hotel first, then sightseeing. Trunk completely empty — even visibly empty bags read as 'laptop went in there.'

lesson.pin_title: Hotel first. Trunk empty. Even empty bags get smashed for. | tabiji.ai
lesson.pin_description: Use attended parking (parc de stationnement gardé) or hotel valet at €5–€15 premium when bags must stay. Carry passports on your person, not the trunk. After a break-in, photograph damage, file a Plainte with Police Nationale within 24 hours, and notify the rental company in the same window.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: Inside a 'POLICE MUNICIPALE de Cannes' office, a uniformed officer in light blue with a navy police cap types on a computer while a woman in a sunhat files a report at the desk. stacked.pin_description: While you're framing the Miroir d'Eau shot, a 'lost tourist' asks for the Cité du Vin and unfolds a map at chest height. Two crew members step into your blind spots — phone slides out, wallet leaves a back pocket. Wear cross-body bags in front; never sling a bag over a chair back at Place du Parlement terrasses.

Panel 1: At Place de la Bourse with the Miroir d'Eau and 18th-century facade behind, a woman in a dark sunhat with a backpack is approached by three young people unfolding a paper map: 'Excuse me — the metro?' Panel 2: They press in closer holding the map at chest height: 'Show me the map!' as her backpack hangs visibly behind her. Panel 3: One of them has unzipped her backpack — she spins around: 'Hands off my bag!' Panel 4: She walks off wearing the same backpack now.

hook.hook: She unfolded the map at chest height. That broke your sightline to your own backpack.

hook.pin_description: Place de la Bourse, the Miroir d'Eau, the 1.2-km Rue Sainte-Catherine, Place du Parlement and Esplanade des Quinconces are the densest pickpocket zones in Bordeaux. Crews target tourists already mid-photo or mid-map specifically because hands and eyes are committed elsewhere.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: At Place de la Bourse in Bordeaux, with the 18th-century Place de la Bourse facade and Miroir d'Eau reflecting behind her, a woman in an orange shirt, dark sunhat and backpack stops as three young people unfold a paper map at her: 'Excuse me — the metro?'

lesson.pin_description: The chair-back hang is a known invitation in Bordeaux café zones. Treat any directions-ask, map-flash or 'do you speak English' approach where the person stands too close as an active distraction. Police Nationale 17 if surrounded; the Police Municipale patrols the historic UNESCO core in summer.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: A woman now wearing her backpack on her front walks past Place de la Bourse and the Miroir d'Eau in Bordeaux, telling another traveler with a smile: 'Wear bags in front in crowds!' The 18th-century classical facade and reflecting pool fill the background.

stacked.headline: TGV from Paris arrives every 20 minutes. The crew works the door-close window.

stacked.pin_description: Five people press onto your TGV vestibule as doors close. Two press in front, two behind, one watches for you to react — the press itself is the cover. Board early rather than rushing, decline all 'help with your bags' offers on the Saint-Jean concourse, keep wallet and phone in a money belt or front zipped pocket.

hook.hook: He wore a high-vis vest. He grabbed your bag at the door. He was on the platform when the doors closed.

hook.pin_description: Saint-Jean is the busiest pickpocket node in Bordeaux because tourist density is high (TGV from Paris every 20 minutes) and crews can hit and disperse before passengers compare notes. The 'helpful porter' in a fake high-vis vest is a recurring variant.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: At Gare de Bordeaux Saint-Jean platform, a woman in an orange shirt, sunhat and backpack steps from train doors holding a water bottle while a man in a bright yellow high-vis vest reaches toward her: 'Let me help, miss!'

lesson.lesson: Carry your own bags. Board early. Decline all 'help' on the Saint-Jean concourse. Money belt for the TGV.

lesson.alt_text: Comic panel four: Inside the airy Gare de Bordeaux Saint-Jean concourse with arched glass roof and station clock tower, a woman in a sunhat now wears her backpack across her front, holding a paper map and standing at a 'Bordeaux Info Desk' counter. Crews work Place de la Bourse, the Miroir d'Eau approach, the Rue Sainte-Catherine pedestrian zone, and around the Cathédrale Saint-André and Tour Pey-Berland. stacked.headline: 'Cross-border counterfeit check.' French PAF doesn't operate inside the city. Ever.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide

stacked.pin_description: Plainclothes 'police' in Petite France quiet streets and at tram stops cite 'cross-border counterfeit checks' because the German border is 5 km away — but French Police aux Frontières only works at official border crossings, never in city tourist zones. Show only a passport copy, demand the carte professionnelle, insist on the commissariat. 17 or 112.

Panel 3: A real uniformed gendarme is now on the bridge in the background; the tourist gestures to the scammer: 'Let's go to the real police!' as the scammer flees.

hook.pin_title: 'Cross-border check' — PAF doesn't work in the city. | Strasbourg
hook.pin_description: The Strasbourg-specific framing exploits the geography: the German border is 5 km east via Pont de l'Europe. But French Police aux Frontières (PAF) operates only at official crossings — Pont de l'Europe vehicle crossing, Entzheim Airport, Gare Centrale international platform — never in the city tourist zones.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: On a quiet Strasbourg street with half-timbered Alsatian houses behind, a grey-bearded man in a denim shirt with brown leather satchel is approached by a younger man in dark clothes holding up a phone-sized fake badge in his palm. stacked.headline: Yellow Euronet ATM. Card stuck. The 'helpful stranger' is reading your PIN.

stacked.pin_description: Yellow Euronet/Travelex ATMs near Cathedral Square and Gare Centrale charge €5–€15 fees plus 'Dynamic Currency Conversion' that costs 4× more than a French bank ATM. Plus skimmers and false-slot inserts. Use BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL, Crédit Agricole or Crédit Mutuel lobby ATMs — and at any DCC prompt, choose 'No, charge in EUR.'

Panel 2: The yellow EUR-ATM closer up — the suit-wearing stranger leans in and points at the keypad: 'Ah, it is stuck? Try your PIN again.' Panel 3: At the same yellow EUR-ATM,

hook.pin_description: The false-slot insert jams your card. The 'helpful' stranger appears within seconds because he was waiting nearby. You enter the PIN twice, give up, walk to find help — and he pulls a thin tool from his pocket and retrieves both the false-slot insert AND your stuck card.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel one: On a Strasbourg street with the Gothic spire of the Cathedral visible in the background, a grey-bearded man in a denim shirt and satchel stands at a yellow standalone 'EUR-ATM' machine bearing a red 'CARD STUCK' label. lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Bank-lobby ATMs only. Decline DCC. | Strasbourg
lesson.pin_description: At any DCC prompt, choose 'No, charge in EUR' so your issuer applies the better rate — DCC adds 5–8% on a Euronet/Travelex withdrawal. Wiggle the slot before inserting; cover the keypad. If your card jams, do NOT leave — call your bank from the ATM and stay until staff arrive.

stacked.headline: "Quick swim!" — your bag is gone in 60 seconds.
stacked.brand_sub: From the France Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Grande Plage bag theft: thieves lift your beach bag while you swim — 60 to 90 seconds
stacked.pin_description: On Grande Plage, Plage Miramar, and Cote des Basques, thieves watch swimmers leave bags on towels and lift them in 60 to 90 seconds, walking off toward Place Bellevue. Bring only what you can lose, use a waterproof neck pouch in the water, and swim in shifts with a friend. Sit near a poste de secours lifeguard station. If hit, file a Plainte within 24 hours.
stacked.alt_text: Four-panel comic. Panel 1: A man on the Grande Plage in Biarritz drops a black tote on a striped towel and shouts "Quick swim!" before running toward the water. Panel 2: A couple in striped shirt and blue dress walk past the towel; the man lifts the tote saying "Tourist bag — easy!" Panel 3: The swimmer returns, dripping, looking at the empty towel: "My bag is gone!" Panel 4: A shop attendant hands him a small zip pouch saying "Beach pouch for valuables!"

hook.hook: Drop your bag, run for a swim. 60 seconds later it is walking toward Place Bellevue.
hook.foot: Beach Blanket Theft at Grande Plage  ·  tabiji.ai
hook.pin_title: Biarritz beach theft hook: 60 seconds is all a Grande Plage thief needs
hook.pin_description: Lift-and-walk crews work the Grande Plage every July and August. The moment the last swimmer in your group hits the water, your tote is gone. Bring only sunscreen and a towel; carry phone, cards, and key in a waterproof neck pouch into the surf. Swim in shifts. Sit near the poste de secours. Lost bag? File the Plainte within 24 hours for insurance.

lesson.pin_title: Grande Plage lesson: take valuables into the water in a sealed pouch
lesson.pin_description: The towel is not a safe. Phone, cards, hotel key, and passport go into a waterproof neck pouch and into the water with you. Leave only what you can afford to lose on the sand. Swim in shifts with a companion, position your towel near the lifeguard, and skip Grande Plage with a backpack full of valuables. If you do get hit, the Plainte must be filed within 24 hours.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel. Inside a beach shop, a smiling attendant holds up a small zippered pouch toward a man with a camera, saying "Beach pouch for valuables!"

stacked.pin_title: Rocher de la Vierge camera-drop scam: photo favor turns into a 300 euro shakedown
stacked.pin_description: Near Rocher de la Vierge and Port Vieux, a stranger hands you a heavy DSLR for a photo. Mid-handoff they fumble, the (already-broken) camera hits the ground, and you owe 200 to 300 euros. Decline politely and point to your own phone. If they corner you, suggest filing a report together: "nous allons porter plainte ensemble." Never pay cash. Police: 17.

hook.pin_description: At Rocher de la Vierge or the Grande Plage promenade, the broken-camera scam runs all summer. Stranger asks for a photo, hands over a too-heavy DSLR, then drops it on you. The camera was already broken; the prop runs all afternoon. Decline, point to your phone, and refuse to pay cash. If pressured, suggest going to the Police Municipale together.

lesson.pin_description: If a stranger insists you hold their camera, the camera is already broken. The fumble is part of the act, the 200-300 euro "replacement" is the goal. Offer to take the photo with your own phone and email it. Never pay cash on the spot. Suggest a joint police report — real owners run, scammers run faster. Walking past a Police Municipale booth is enough.

stacked.pin_description: At ATMs near Casino Barriere, Avenue Edouard VII, Les Halles, and Biarritz station, a stranger leans in with a paper map asking for help while an accomplice or pinhole camera reads your PIN. Cards have been cloned and re-used in Bucharest and Sofia within 48 hours. Use bank-lobby ATMs in business hours, wiggle the slot, cover the keypad, and decline all "helpful" advice.

"Wins" go to crew members with marked bills; tourists lose 50-500 euros in five minutes. The lookout whistles, the cardboard table folds in 20 seconds. The crowd around the table includes pickpockets — keep moving.

hook.pin_description: The cardboard box on the Biarritz boardwalk is staffed by four people: operator, lookout, roper, and shills who fan euro bills to pull you in. Marked bills, sleight of hand, and a 20-second pack-up when the lookout whistles "police." You cannot win it back. The crowd around it is also seeded with pickpockets. Walk straight past.

lesson.pin_title: Biarritz lesson: street gambling is illegal in France — never bet on the boardwalk
lesson.pin_description: There is no version where you win. The operator, lookout, roper, and shills are coordinated. Marked bills come back to the bag. The crowd is salted with pickpockets, so even watching is a risk. Keep your hand on your bag and walk past. Want to see Biarritz? Stick to the Casino terraces and Rocher de la Vierge — leave the cardboard box behind.

stacked.pin_description: Near Port Vieux and late-night Biarritz, friendly "locals" steer solo tourists into a side-street bar with no posted prices. Drinks come in at 25-40 euros each (normal: 10-15), the friends leave 20 euros and vanish, and bouncers walk you to an ATM. Choose your own bars (Le Bar Jean, Le Surfing, Eden Rock Cafe). Check posted prices before sitting. Pay by credit card so you can chargeback.

The new friends drop 20 euros and disappear. Bouncers walk you to an ATM. The fix: pick your own bar (4.5+ Google rating), check posted prices, and stay in pairs.

lesson.pin_description: Bars without a posted menu are not for you. Pick venues with a printed list out front (Le Bar Jean, Le Surfing, Eden Rock Cafe). Pay by credit card so you have chargeback options. Refuse to pay an inflated bill without police: "j'appelle la police." Stay in pairs, tell your hotel where you are going, and treat any "new friend" who insists on a specific bar as a recruiter.

Theft spikes 3-5x in summer. Wear a cross-body bag with the opening against your body, hand on top. Wallet in the front pocket or money belt — never the back pocket. Bring 20-50 euros cash and leave cards at the hotel. Saturday 9 AM-12 PM is peak.

hook.pin_description: The crowded aisles of Les Halles de Biarritz are perfect for a one-bump lift. Tourists lean in to admire the jambon de Bayonne while a pickpocket presses past, takes the wallet, and disappears toward the door. Theft spikes 3-5x in summer; Saturday morning is peak. stacked.pin_title: Biarritz Airport (BIQ) taxi scam: terminal touts charge 40 euros for a 25 euro ride
stacked.pin_description: At Biarritz-Pays Basque Airport (BIQ) and the train station, unmarked-car touts inside the terminal quote 40-60 euros for a 25 euro daytime fare. No meter, no license, cash only, no receipts. Walk past them to the official rank, ask for "au compteur, s'il vous plait," and confirm Tarif A (day) or Tarif B (night/Sunday/holiday). Or take Chronoplus bus C5 — 1.20 euros, 20-25 minutes, every 20 minutes.

The official taxi rank is signed "Taxis Officiels" — meters in front, Tarif A daytime, Tarif B night/Sunday/holiday. Ask "au compteur, s'il vous plait" and note the carte professionnelle number. The clipboard sits at chest height so your eyes are down; the second crew member works your shoulder bag from behind. Real French charities have a stall at Monoprix or the Mairie, branded bibs, and collect emails — not signatures. Say "non, merci" without slowing.

stacked.pin_description: At Cote des Basques, Plage de la Milady, and remote surf-spot lots, professional crews target rentals (sterile interiors, GPS marks, bags visible). A concealed reader inside a stranger's bag pulls contactless data through leather wallets at 2-10cm range. French €50 single-tap limit means three €49 charges fly under most fraud thresholds. Use RFID-blocking sleeves (€10-€30) or set the contactless limit to €0 in your bank app.

Walk to the Sitio counter inside arrivals for a printed flat-rate receipt. From the Tabiji Mexico Scam Survival Guide.

hook.pin_description: If a guy in a TAXI vest pulls you off the arrivals floor at MEX with "800 pesos to your hotel," you're paying triple. The real prepaid Sitio fare to Zona Centro is MX$280 — buy the boleto pre-pagado at the Sitio Taxi counter inside the terminal. Tabiji's Mexico scam guide.

lesson.pin_description: Mexico City's authorized airport taxis (Sitio 300, Porto Taxi, Nueva Imagen) sell prepaid flat-rate tickets at counters inside the arrivals hall — Zona Centro MX$280, Polanco MX$250. Anyone selling rides on the curb or pulling you off the floor is a tout at 2–3x. More CDMX defenses from Tabiji.

stacked.pin_description: In Roma Norte, Condesa, and Polanco, some Uber/Didi drivers WhatsApp "app is broken, you pay here" mid-trip and demand cash at 2–3x the in-app fare. Pay only inside the app, never hand the driver your physical card, and cancel any driver requesting WhatsApp before pickup. From the Tabiji Mexico Scam Survival Guide.

hook.pin_description: If your CDMX Uber or Didi driver messages "app broken, WhatsApp please" before pickup, cancel and rebook. The next move is a 2–3x cash demand or a card-reader "manual entry" cloning. Pay in-app only — and never hand the driver your physical card. Tabiji's Mexico scam guide.

stacked.pin_description: After 10 PM in Roma Norte, Condesa, and Coyoacán, officers (often Policía Auxiliar) approach tourists with "Buenas noches. Document check, please," then invent infractions and demand MX$500–MX$5,000 cash. Real Mexican fines are written tickets paid at a delegación. Say "podemos ir a la delegación" and ask for the badge number. From the Tabiji Mexico Scam Survival Guide.

Document check, please," they declare "This is a big problem. Pay cash now," he holds up his passport and says "No. We can go to the delegación," then later texts the embassy from inside an OXXO with the lesson "Real fines are never paid in cash."

hook.hook: Real Mexican police don't take cash on the street.
hook.pin_title: CDMX fake-police rule: real fines aren't paid in cash
hook.pin_description: Any CDMX officer demanding cash on the street after a "document check" is running the shakedown. Real Mexican fines are written tickets paid at a delegación. Say "podemos ir a la delegación" and "quiero hablar con el consulado" — fake officers usually bail at the consulate mention. Tabiji's Mexico scam guide.

lesson.pin_description: Two phrases break the CDMX fake-police shakedown: "podemos ir a la delegación" (we can go to the precinct) and "quiero hablar con el consulado" (I want to call the consulate). Show a passport photocopy, never the original; never unlock your phone. Save US Embassy +52 55 8526 2561. More Mexico defenses from Tabiji.

stacked.headline: The taxi "ATM nearby" detour that empties three accounts.

stacked.pin_title: Mexico City secuestro exprés: refuse every taxi "ATM nearby" offer
stacked.pin_description: Express kidnapping (secuestro exprés) starts with a Polanco or Roma taxi driver saying "sorry, cash only — ATM is right here" and parking at a standalone street ATM. Two or three accomplices appear, force the victim through multi-bank withdrawals, average loss tops US$1,000. Use only ATMs inside HSBC, Banamex, BBVA, or Santander branches in business hours. From the Tabiji Mexico Scam Survival Guide.

Now," then he files a denuncia at a Policía station with the lesson "Only use ATMs inside banks or stores."

hook.pin_description: Mexico City express kidnappings (secuestro exprés) almost always start at a standalone street ATM the taxi "happens" to find. "Sorry, cash only" and "ATM nearby" are the warning phrases. Use ATMs only inside bank branches in business hours; set a MX$3,000 daily limit before travel. Tabiji's Mexico scam guide.

Set a MX$3,000 (US$175) daily limit, withdraw MX$1,000 max per transaction, refuse every "home currency" DCC prompt. More CDMX defenses from Tabiji.

Oaxaca offices quoting MX$8,000–MX$15,000 "standard" deposits hold the funds 30–60 days or never refund, then layer "pre-existing damage" claims on top. Use Hertz, Europcar, or Budget at the airport — and refuse anything over US$500 on a credit card (never debit). Tabiji's Mexico scam guide.

Real fish tacos are MX$45 two blocks away. Ask for the menu en espanol, eat on Avenida 15, and refuse card surcharges over 3%.

stacked.pin_description: Touts at the Great Pyramid of Cholula sell 'mandatory tunnel guides' at MX$500/person and demand a MX$100 'church fee' on top — both fake. Palafox during business hours, set a MX$3,000 daily limit with transaction alerts, and exchange USD only at reputable casas de cambio (Forex on Av. Palafox y Mendoza, DYNER) — not hotel reception. scams.scam_name: Altstadt Kölsch Bar Overcharge & Köbes Bill-Padding

stacked.headline: "Ten beers? And a 'service fee'?"
stacked.brand_sub: From the Germany Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Cologne Köbes Bill-Padding — How Tally Marks and a 'Servicegebühr' Double Your Tab
stacked.pin_description: In tourist-trap Altstadt brauhäuser, Köbes waiters keep refilling your 0.2L Kölsch (€4–€5 vs. €2.50–€3 at real Hausbrauereien), pad the coaster tally, and add a 10–15% 'Servicegebühr.' Cover your glass with the coaster to stop service. Drink at Brauhaus Päffgen, Früh am Dom, Gaffel Haus, Peters Brauhaus, or Sünner im Walfisch. Tip 5–10% in cash.

Panel 2: the Köbes carries a tray of fresh beers, 'Another for you, mein Herr!' Panel 3: the tourist holds a long bill, 'Ten beers? And a service fee?' Panel 4: at Früh am Dom he places a coaster on top of the empty glass, 'Always cover the glass to stop!'

hook.hook: "Another for you, mein Herr!"
hook.pin_title: Cologne Kölsch trap: the Köbes refills until you cover the glass
hook.pin_description: A Kölsch is 0.2L and traditionally the Köbes never stops bringing them. In tourist-strip Altstadt bars that means €4–€5 a beer, padded coaster tallies, and a sneaky 10–15% 'Servicegebühr.' Cover the glass with the coaster to stop, and drink at the real Hausbrauereien — Päffgen, Früh am Dom, Gaffel, Peters, Sünner im Walfisch.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel: a Köbes in a long blue apron approaches a smiling tourist with a wooden tray of fresh Kölsch glasses inside a packed Cologne brauhaus. Caption: 'Another for you, mein Herr!'

lesson.lesson: Coaster on the glass means stop. Real Kölsch is €2.50–€3 at Päffgen and Früh.

lesson.pin_title: Cologne Kölsch rule: coaster on the glass, drink at Päffgen or Früh am Dom
lesson.pin_description: The coaster is the off switch. Cover the empty glass and the Köbes stops refilling. Check tally marks before paying, refuse unordered Brezel with 'Ich habe das nicht bestellt,' and tip 5–10% in cash — never an added percentage. Real-price Kölsch lives at Brauhaus Päffgen, Früh am Dom, Gaffel Haus, and Peters Brauhaus.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel: tourist places a beer coaster on top of his empty glass at Früh am Dom, smiling Köbes in the background. Caption: 'Always cover the glass to stop!'

Visit 10am–noon or after 7pm.

Panel 4: a Polizei officer beside a Stollen stand says, 'Never let strangers distract you.'

scams.scam_name: Fake VVO Ticket Inspector Cash-Fine Scam

stacked.headline: "Not validated! €60 fine. Cash now."
stacked.brand_sub: From the Germany Scam Survival Guide
stacked.pin_title: Dresden Fake VVO Inspector — Real Inspectors Never Demand Cash
stacked.pin_description: On Dresden trams (Linien 1–13), DVB buses, and the S1/S2/S3, plain-clothes impostors demand €60 cash on the spot. A real VVO inspector issues a printed Erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt with a 2-week bank-transfer slip. Demand the Dienstausweis. Validate every single ticket at the blue box on board. DVB 0351-857-11-11.

Panel 2: he points at a ticket, 'Not validated! €60 fine. Cash now.' Panel 3: tourist asks calmly, 'Dienstausweis? Your official ID?' Panel 4: a uniformed VVO inspector beside him says, 'Real inspectors never demand only cash.'

hook.hook: "Not validated! €60 fine. Cash now."
hook.pin_title: Dresden tram "inspector" demanding €60 in cash is a scammer
hook.pin_description: Plain clothes, no Dienstausweis, fast euro count — that's the fake VVO inspector. Real inspectors give you a printed Erhöhtes Beförderungsentgelt and a 14-day bank transfer option. Stay calm, ask for the Dienstausweis photo ID, refuse to hand over cash.
hook.alt_text: Comic panel: a man in plain clothes points at a small ticket held by a tourist on a Dresden tram platform. Caption: 'Not validated! €60 fine. Cash now.'

lesson.lesson: Dienstausweis or no fine. Validate at the blue box on the tram.
lesson.foot: tabiji.ai  ·  Real scams from real travelers
lesson.pin_title: Dresden transit rule: ask for the Dienstausweis, validate at the blue box
lesson.pin_description: VVO Tarifzone 10 covers central Dresden. Validate your single ticket at the blue box ON the tram or bus before the first stop, keep the receipt, and if anyone asks for cash demand the Dienstausweis. Real fines come on paper with a bank transfer slip — never cash on the platform. DVB hotline 0351-857-11-11.
lesson.alt_text: Comic panel: a real VVO inspector in a navy uniform stands beside the tourist, holding up his official Dienstausweis ID badge. Caption: 'Real inspectors never demand only cash.'
